country.name: Austria
country.summary: Austria grows wine on its eastern side, where the Alps give out and the land slopes to the Pannonian plain. Four federal states carry it all: Niederösterreich along the Danube and north of Vienna, Burgenland down the Hungarian border, Steiermark in the south east and the city of Wien itself. Grüner Veltliner is the flag, about a third of the vineyard, dry and white peppered; Riesling is dry and fuller than Germany's; Zweigelt is the everyday red and Blaufränkisch the serious one. The law runs Wein, Landwein, Qualitätswein, Prädikatswein, with Kabinett a dry Qualitätswein class, and the DAC system lays a grape and style over each region's name. The Wachau's own Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd are a growers' scale of weight. Most Austrian wine is dry; the sweet exception lives beside the shallow Neusiedlersee.
country.overview:
Vines came to Austria with the Celts and were organised by the Romans; the monasteries of the Middle Ages planted the Danube terraces and the Leitha hills; Vienna grew up as a wine town with vineyards inside its walls. The modern story turns on 1985, when a handful of brokers were caught sweetening cheap wine with diethylene glycol. Exports collapsed, and the strict wine law that followed rebuilt the trade on dry, estate bottled wine of real origin, every Qualitätswein carrying a state control number and the red white red seal. Austria joined the European Union in 1995 and built its appellation system, the DAC, from 2002 onward.

The geography is simple to hold. Niederösterreich, Lower Austria, carries most of the vineyard: the Wachau, Kremstal, Kamptal, Traisental and Wagram along and above the Danube, the broad Weinviertel to the north, Carnuntum east of Vienna and the Thermenregion south of it. Burgenland runs down the Hungarian border and is red and sweet wine country around the Neusiedlersee and the hills beyond it. Steiermark, Styria, is steep, green and rainy, the home of Sauvignon Blanc. Wien farms commercial vineyard within the city limits. The climate across all of it is continental with a Pannonian pull from the east: hot dry summers, cold winters, cold nights that keep the acidity.

The law has four rungs. Wein is the plain table wine, Landwein the protected geographical indication from one of three Landwein areas, Qualitätswein the protected origin from a named region, and Prädikatswein the ripeness ladder, picked at a certified must weight in Klosterneuburger Mostwaage degrees and never chaptalised or sweetened. Kabinett in Austria is a dry Qualitätswein category with a cap on alcohol and sugar, not a Prädikat. A DAC, Districtus Austriae Controllatus, is a Qualitätswein whose region name may only be used for the grapes and style the region has chosen as typical; the older DACs rank wines as Klassik and Reserve, the newer ones as Gebietswein, Ortswein and Riedenwein, and since the Thermenregion joined in 2023 every specific wine growing region has one. The word Ried marks a single vineyard on every label.

The exam leans on Grüner Veltliner's tell of white pepper and lentil, on the Wachau's three categories and their alcohol lines, on which grape each DAC names, on Zweigelt's parentage and on the sweet wines of Rust and the Seewinkel. A server needs less: that Austrian means dry unless the label says otherwise, that Smaragd is the full one, and that Blaufränkisch is a peppery, bright red worth pouring with duck.
ladder: The base: Austrian wine with no closer origin; a grape and a vintage may be named.
The protected geographical indication, from one of three Landwein areas: Weinland (Niederösterreich, Burgenland and Wien), Steirerland (Steiermark) and Bergland (the alpine west).

Protected origin from a named generic or specific region, minimum 15° KMW, passed by a tasting panel; it carries a state control number and the red white red Banderole; chaptalisation is allowed within limits.
A Qualitätswein category, not a Prädikat: at least 17° KMW, no chaptalisation, at most 13% alcohol and 9 grams of residual sugar; in Austria it reads as dry and light.

No chaptalisation, no sweetening; must weight certified at picking: Spätlese 19° KMW, Auslese 21, Beerenauslese and Eiswein 25, Strohwein or Schilfwein 25, Trockenbeerenauslese 30; Ausbruch survives only as Ruster Ausbruch DAC at 30.

Districtus Austriae Controllatus: a Qualitätswein whose regional name is tied to the region's typical grapes and style; Klassik and Reserve in the older DACs, Gebietswein, Ortswein and Riedenwein in the newer.

The protected sparkling wine pyramid: Klassik (nine months on lees, grapes from one federal state), Reserve (eighteen months, traditional method, hand picked), Grosse Reserve (thirty months, traditional method, one municipality).
labels: Dry: at most 4 grams of residual sugar, or up to 9 when the acidity is within 2 grams of the sugar; the default style of the country.
Off dry, up to 12 grams of residual sugar; Lieblich runs to 45 and Süss above that.
A single vineyard; the word must stand in front of any vineyard name on the label.
A Qualitätswein of at least 13% alcohol; in the older DACs the dry upper rung above Klassik, released later.
The fresh, unoaked rung of an older DAC, or a Styrian grower's word for the same style.
Regional, village and single vineyard wine: the origin pyramid the newer DACs use.
The red white red strip on the capsule of every Qualitätswein, with the state control number on the label.
Klosterneuburger Mostwaage, the Austrian must weight scale: one degree is one per cent sugar by weight; 17 KMW is about 83 Oechsle.
A grower's tavern pouring its own new wine under a pine bough, and the young wine itself.
Grape must still fermenting, cloudy and sweet, sold for a few weeks each autumn.
A field blend: several grapes co planted, picked and fermented together; a Vienna speciality with its own DAC.

A first class vineyard: 1ÖTW is the private mark of the Österreichische Traditionsweingüter, the growers' body of the Danube regions; since the 2023 wine law Erste Lage and Grosse Lage are also legal terms for Rieden a DAC region classifies, hand picked and within the yield limit.

grapes.name: Grüner Veltliner
grapes.styles: About a third of the vineyard, a natural crossing of Traminer with a vine found at St. Georgen in Burgenland: white pepper, lentil and radish over green apple and citrus, from litre bottle Heuriger wine to the age worthy Smaragd of the Wachau; always dry by default.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: A small share but the prestige white of the Danube terraces: dry, stony, fuller than the Mosel, apricot and lime on gneiss, built to age.

grapes.name: Zweigelt
grapes.styles: Austria's most planted red, bred in 1922 at Klosterneuburg from Blaufränkisch and St. Laurent: sour cherry, soft tannin, juicy and chillable, with a serious Reserve face around the Neusiedlersee.

grapes.name: Blaufränkisch
grapes.styles: The structured red: dark cherry, black pepper, iron and bright acidity, from Mittelburgenland, Leithaberg and Eisenberg; Lemberger in Germany, Kékfrankos in Hungary.

grapes.name: Welschriesling
grapes.styles: No relation to Riesling: light, crisp and neutral for Styrian spritz and Sekt bases, and the great botrytis grape of the Seewinkel's sweet wines.

grapes.name: Pinot Blanc
grapes.styles: Weissburgunder here: creamy, quiet whites along the Leithaberg and in Styria, and a Sekt base.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Called Morillon in Styria, where it is lean and mineral; richer and oak aged on the Leithaberg; a part of many sweet blends by the lake.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Styria's signature: gooseberry, elderflower and wet stone in the fresh style, smoky and dense from the classified Rieden.

grapes.name: St. Laurent
grapes.styles: A Pinot relative and Zweigelt's other parent: silky, dark fruited and fragrant, best in the Thermenregion and by the lake.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Blauburgunder or Blauer Burgunder: a quiet but growing presence in the Thermenregion, on the Leithaberg and in Carnuntum.

grapes.name: Neuburger
grapes.styles: A natural crossing of Roter Veltliner and Silvaner: nutty, broad and soft, at home in the Wachau and on the Leithaberg.

grapes.name: Roter Veltliner
grapes.styles: An old pink skinned grape, no relation to Grüner, that gives full, spicy, long lived whites on the loess of the Wagram.

grapes.name: Rotgipfler
grapes.styles: A Thermenregion native, rich and apricot scented, often blended with Zierfandler for the old Gumpoldskirchner style.

grapes.name: Zierfandler
grapes.styles: Also Spätrot, the Thermenregion's other native: spicy, honeyed and capable of age, dry or sweet.

grapes.name: Blauer Wildbacher
grapes.styles: The Weststeiermark's red grape, almost always made as Schilcher, a shrill, high acid rosé, still or sparkling.

exam: Name the four rungs of Austrian law and place Kabinett correctly as a dry Qualitätswein category, not a Prädikat.
Know the Prädikat must weights in KMW and that Ausbruch now belongs to Rust alone as Ruster Ausbruch DAC.
Give the grape or grapes each DAC names: Weinviertel, Kamptal, Kremstal, Traisental, Wachau, Mittelburgenland, Eisenberg, Leithaberg, Neusiedlersee, Wiener Gemischter Satz.
Recite the Wachau's Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd with their alcohol lines and know that they are a growers' scale, not national law.
Hold Grüner Veltliner's tell (white pepper, lentil, radish) against Sauvignon Blanc and dry Riesling in a blind flight.
Give Zweigelt's parents, its date and its birthplace, and tell it from Blaufränkisch by structure.
Place the Neusiedlersee, explain why it breeds botrytis and name the sweet styles made on its shores.
traps: Austrian Kabinett is dry and capped at 13% alcohol; it is a Qualitätswein class, the opposite of Germany's off dry Prädikat.
Welschriesling is not Riesling and Roter Veltliner is not a red Grüner Veltliner; neither grape is related to the one it sounds like.
Smaragd, Federspiel and Steinfeder are the Vinea Wachau's categories and mean nothing outside the Wachau.
Ausbruch is no longer a Prädikat anywhere: since the 2020 vintage it is Ruster Ausbruch DAC, picked at Trockenbeerenauslese ripeness, from Rust only.
Zweigelt is a 1922 crossing, not an ancient vine; Blaufränkisch is the old one, and the parent.
Gemischter Satz is a field blend grown together, not a cuvée blended in the cellar.
A DAC is a Qualitätswein with a style attached; a region's name used for a grape outside its DAC list falls back to the generic Niederösterreich, Burgenland, Steiermark or Wien.

About a third of the vineyard; Traminer crossed with the St. Georgen vine; white pepper, lentil, radish over green apple and citrus; dry by default.
Blaufränkisch crossed with St. Laurent, 1922, Klosterneuburg. Austria's most planted red: sour cherry, soft tannin, juicy.

cards.f: The DAC system in one line
cards.b: Districtus Austriae Controllatus, from 2002: a region name reserved for its typical grapes and style; Klassik and Reserve in the older DACs, Gebietswein, Ortswein, Riedenwein in the newer.

Niederösterreich (most of the vineyard, the Danube and the Weinviertel), Burgenland (reds and sweets by the Neusiedlersee), Steiermark (Sauvignon Blanc on steep hills), Wien (vineyard inside the capital).
Klassik: nine months on lees, one federal state. Reserve: eighteen months, traditional method, hand picked. Grosse Reserve: thirty months, traditional method, one municipality.

cards.f: Trocken in Austria: the sugar line
cards.b: At most 4 g/l residual sugar, or up to 9 g/l when total acidity is within 2 g/l of the sugar. Halbtrocken runs to 12.
The diethylene glycol scandal: exports collapsed, a strict wine law followed with state control numbers and the Banderole, and Austria rebuilt on dry estate wine.

questions.q: Which Austrian category is a dry Qualitätswein class rather than a Prädikat?
questions.exp: Austrian law places Kabinett inside Qualitätswein with a cap of 13% alcohol and 9 g/l sugar; Spätlese, Auslese and Eiswein are Prädikat levels defined by must weight.

questions.q: Which two grapes were crossed to breed Zweigelt at Klosterneuburg in 1922?
questions.exp: Zweigelt is Blaufränkisch crossed with St. Laurent, bred in 1922 and now Austria's most planted red; it is softer and juicier than its Blaufränkisch parent.

questions.q: What is the minimum must weight, in KMW, for an Austrian Trockenbeerenauslese?
questions.exp: Trockenbeerenauslese and Ruster Ausbruch DAC both start at 30° KMW; Beerenauslese and Eiswein at 25; Auslese at 21.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation DAC stand for on an Austrian label?
questions.exp: Districtus Austriae Controllatus is the Latin name of Austria's protected origin system, begun with the Weinviertel in 2002, tying a region's name to its typical grapes and style.

questions.q: Which federal state holds the largest share of Austria's vineyard?
questions.exp: Niederösterreich, Lower Austria, carries most of the vineyard: the Danube regions, the Weinviertel, Carnuntum and the Thermenregion; Burgenland is second, Steiermark third, and Oberösterreich has only a few vines.

questions.q: Which town alone may put the word Ausbruch on a wine label?
questions.exp: Since the 2020 vintage Ausbruch survives only as Ruster Ausbruch DAC: botrytised berries hand picked at 30° KMW, grown and made in Rust on the lake's west shore. Illmitz and Gols lie across the water, and Mörbisch, Rust's neighbour, has no claim to the word.

questions.q: Which grape takes about a third of Austria's vineyard?
questions.exp: Grüner Veltliner is the country's most planted grape by a wide margin; Zweigelt leads the reds, Welschriesling is second among whites and Riesling is a small, prestigious share.

questions.q: Which word must stand before a single vineyard name on an Austrian label?
questions.exp: Ried marks a registered single vineyard, as in Ried Heiligenstein or Ried Kellerberg, so that a vineyard is never confused with a village or a brand.

regions.name: Wachau / Kamptal / Kremstal
regions.summary: Three separate regions of Niederösterreich sharing the Danube, two grapes and one idea. The Wachau is the gorge between Melk and Krems, gneiss terraces above the river, with its own growers' scale of Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd and, since the 2020 vintage, a DAC. The Kremstal wraps the town of Krems, primary rock on the west side and deep loess to the east. The Kamptal runs north up the Kamp river through Langenlois, with the Heiligenstein above Zöbing as its great Riesling hill. In all three Grüner Veltliner takes the loess and Riesling the bare rock, the wines are dry, and the DACs name only those two grapes at the top.

terroir.climate: Two weathers meet over the Danube: cool, damp air from the Waldviertel forest to the north west and warm, dry Pannonian air from the east. Summers are warm, nights cold, and the swing between them holds acidity in ripe grapes. The Wachau's side valleys, the Spitzer Graben above all, are the coolest corners; the Kremstal's loess east of Krems and the lower Kamptal are warmer.
terroir.soils: Primary rock on the slopes: gneiss, amphibolite and granulite of the Bohemian Massif, weathered to thin, stony soils that hold little water and ripen Riesling. Loess, the wind blown dust of the ice ages, lies deep on the gentler ground and the terraces' upper edges, holding water and lime and suiting Grüner Veltliner. The Kremstal east of Krems is almost all loess; the Kamptal adds the Heiligenstein's Permian desert sandstone with volcanic grit.
terroir.topography: The Wachau is a gorge, the river cutting through the hills so that the vineyards hang on dry stone walled terraces at slopes too steep for machines, most facing south on the north bank. At Krems the valley opens into a basin of loess hills. The Kamptal is a broad north running side valley; the Heiligenstein and the Gaisberg rise above Zöbing and Kammern, with the Lamm and the Grub lying at their feet.
terroir.water: The Danube itself: it reflects light onto the terraces, stores warmth, and its mists in autumn help Riesling ripen without rot. The Kamp and the Krems rivers draw cold air down their valleys at night and let the Pannonian warmth in by day.

grapes.name: Grüner Veltliner
grapes.styles: The majority grape of all three regions, planted on loess and the richer terraces: white pepper, lentil and green apple as Steinfeder or Federspiel, honeyed, broad and smoky as Smaragd and Reserve, able to age for decades.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: The prestige grape of the bare primary rock terraces and the Heiligenstein: dry, apricot and lime, stony and taut, fuller than the Mosel and built to age twenty years.

grapes.name: Pinot Blanc
grapes.styles: Weissburgunder: creamy, quiet, allowed in the Wachau DAC's regional and village tiers but never as a Riedenwein; in the Kamptal and Kremstal it is sold outside the DAC as Niederösterreich Qualitätswein.

grapes.name: Neuburger
grapes.styles: Old Wachau speciality, nutty and soft, kept by a few estates for Federspiel and Smaragd.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Grown in small amounts for the Wachau DAC's regional and village tiers and for the Kamptal's traditional method Sekt.

grapes.name: Roter Veltliner
grapes.styles: The Wagram's loess grape, spicy and long lived, met at the Kremstal's eastern edge.

grapes.name: Zweigelt
grapes.styles: A little red for the Heuriger table and the regional tier of the Wachau DAC; in the Kremstal and Kamptal it is sold as Niederösterreich Qualitätswein.

wines.note: The full, dry top of the Wachau scale, at least 12.5% alcohol: Grüner Veltliner shows honey, white pepper and smoke, Riesling apricot and crushed stone. Serve at cellar temperature, not ice cold, with roast poultry, veal or a rich fish.
The middle rung, 11.5 to 12.5% alcohol: the classic dry Wachau glass, taut and mineral. Pours well by the glass and fits trout, asparagus and lighter plates.
The lightest category, at most 11.5% alcohol, named after a feathery grass of the terraces; fresh, drunk young and rarely exported.
Dry, lime and white peach, with a flinty edge from the Heiligenstein's sandstone; Reserve bottlings are riper and longer lived.
Pepper, pear and a saline finish; the Lamm gives the richest version. A natural match for Wiener Schnitzel and for anything with dill or horseradish.
Grüner Veltliner and Riesling from Krems, Stein, Senftenberg and the loess villages: a shade softer than the Wachau, often the better value, dry and food friendly.
Traditional method sparkling from Langenlois estates, crisp, apple scented, a sound aperitif.

made.viticulture: The Wachau's terraces are the whole story of its viticulture: dry stone walls, some medieval, hold shallow soil on slopes that can only be worked by hand, so costs are high and yields are low. Vines are trained on wires in the usual Austrian way, and growers of the Vinea Wachau pick by hand under their Codex; the Wachau DAC makes hand harvest the law for every tier. Grüner Veltliner goes onto the loess and the lower, deeper terraces, Riesling onto the bare gneiss at the top where water is scarce and the sun is strongest. Riesling is picked late, often into late October, and a touch of botrytis is tolerated in a Smaragd but not sought. In the Kamptal and Kremstal the gentler loess slopes allow machines and higher yields for the regional tier, while the classified Rieden of the Österreichische Traditionsweingüter, marked 1ÖTW, are farmed to the same standard as the Wachau terraces.
made.winemaking: The style is dry, clean and unoaked. Grapes are pressed whole or after a short skin contact, the must settled, and fermentation runs cool in stainless steel or in large old oak casks that add no flavour; new barriques are rare and the Wachau DAC's village and vineyard tiers may show no obvious oak. Wines are left on fine lees over the winter for texture and bottled in spring, the Reserve and Smaragd later. Chaptalisation is banned under the Vinea Wachau Codex and for Wachau Riedenwein; the Codex also bans concentration and any aromatising. The Wachau's categories are set by alcohol because the wines are dry: Steinfeder up to 11.5%, Federspiel 11.5 to 12.5%, Smaragd from 12.5%. The Kamptal and Kremstal DACs define a Klassik, fresh and without wood or botrytis character, and a Reserve of at least 13% alcohol where a little of both is allowed.

law.classification: All three regions are specific wine growing regions of Niederösterreich with their own DAC. Kremstal DAC came with the 2007 vintage and Kamptal DAC with 2008, both for Grüner Veltliner and Riesling alone, first as Klassik and Reserve and now also in the origin pyramid of Gebietswein, Ortswein and Riedenwein. The Wachau DAC, from the 2020 vintage, lists 17 grapes for its Gebietswein, 9 for its Ortswein from 22 named villages, and only Grüner Veltliner and Riesling for its Riedenwein from registered single vineyards; every tier is hand picked. Beside the DAC the Vinea Wachau, a growers' association founded in 1983, keeps its three categories, Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd, which may be printed together with the DAC.
tiers: Gebietswein
Regional wine of the DAC: in the Wachau from 17 permitted grapes; in Kamptal and Kremstal Grüner Veltliner or Riesling.
Ortswein
Village wine: the village name on the label; nine grapes in the Wachau, each as a single variety.
Riedenwein
Single vineyard wine, Ried before the name; in the Wachau only Grüner Veltliner and Riesling, never chaptalised.
Klassik
Kamptal and Kremstal DAC's fresh rung: dry, no wood or botrytis character, moderate alcohol.
Reserve
Kamptal and Kremstal DAC's upper rung: at least 13% alcohol, dry, a touch of wood or botrytis allowed, released later.
Steinfeder
Vinea Wachau's lightest category, at most 11.5% alcohol, named for a feathery grass of the terraces.
Federspiel
Vinea Wachau's middle category, 11.5 to 12.5% alcohol, named for a falconer's lure.
Smaragd
Vinea Wachau's fullest category, from 12.5% alcohol, named for the emerald lizard that suns itself on the walls.
labels: The Wachau growers' association, founded 1983, whose Codex bans chaptalisation, concentration and aromatising.

Erste Lage of the Österreichische Traditionsweingüter: a vineyard the growers' association classifies as a first class site in the Kamptal, Kremstal, Traisental, Wagram, Carnuntum or Wien. Since the 2023 wine law Erste Lage and Grosse Lage are also legal terms for Rieden a DAC region classifies under its own rules.
Old vines; no legal minimum age, an estate's own word.
Terraces: a cuvée from terraced sites rather than one Ried.

places.name: Wachau
places.note: The Danube gorge from Melk to Krems, a UNESCO World Heritage landscape since 2000: terraced gneiss on the north bank, loess at the terraces' foot, Riesling and Grüner Veltliner graded as Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd and, since 2020, Wachau DAC.

places.name: Spitz
places.note: The coolest of the main villages, at the mouth of the Spitzer Graben: the Singerriedel and Hochrain terraces for Riesling, the Tausendeimerberg above the town, and the Honivogl site on deeper ground by the river for Grüner Veltliner.

places.name: Weissenkirchen
places.note: The heart of Wachau Riesling: the Achleiten, a steep amphibolite and gneiss slope, the Klaus beside it and the Steinriegl above; Joching and Wösendorf are its neighbouring hamlets.

places.name: Dürnstein
places.note: The postcard village under its ruined castle, where the Kellerberg rises in gneiss terraces that give the Wachau's most sought Riesling and Grüner Veltliner Smaragd; the Domäne Wachau cooperative has its cellars here.

places.name: Loiben
places.note: Unterloiben and Oberloiben at the eastern, warmest end: the broad Loibenberg, the Schütt beneath the cliff and the Steinertal, with the Wachau's ripest, fullest Smaragd wines.

places.name: Mautern
places.note: On the south bank opposite Stein, a Roman fort town; its vineyards on the gentler bank give a cooler, finer line of Riesling and Grüner Veltliner.

places.name: Spitzer Graben
places.note: The side valley running north west from Spitz, the coolest and latest ripening corner of the Wachau, mica schist rather than gneiss, Steinfeder and Federspiel country.

places.name: Kremstal
places.note: The valley and basin around Krems, Kremstal DAC since 2007 for Grüner Veltliner and Riesling: primary rock terraces at Krems and Stein in the west, deep loess at Rohrendorf and Gedersdorf in the east, and the south bank around the abbey of Göttweig.

places.name: Krems and Stein
places.note: The twin towns at the gorge's mouth: the Pfaffenberg and the Hund are gneiss terraces at Stein continuous with the Wachau's, giving Riesling of Wachau quality under a Kremstal label.

places.name: Senftenberg
places.note: Up the Krems river north of the town, a steep gneiss gorge of its own: the Pellingen, Hochäcker and Piri terraces give tense, long lived Riesling and Grüner Veltliner.

places.name: Rohrendorf and Gedersdorf
places.note: The loess villages east of Krems, where Grüner Veltliner is broad and generous and Roter Veltliner appears; the Kremstal's bigger estates and the cooperative draw on these slopes.

places.name: Göttweig and Furth
places.note: The south bank beneath the Benedictine abbey of Göttweig, founded in 1083: loess and gravel over rock, warmer and softer wines.

places.name: Kamptal
places.note: The Kamp valley north of the Danube around Langenlois, Austria's largest wine town; Kamptal DAC since 2008 for Grüner Veltliner and Riesling, with the Heiligenstein above Zöbing as its great cru.

places.name: Langenlois
places.note: The market town that gives the Kamptal its estates: the Käferberg, Steinmassl, Loiserberg, Spiegel and Dechant Rieden spread around it on loess, gneiss and gravel.

places.name: Zöbing and the Heiligenstein
places.note: The Heiligenstein is a hill of Permian sandstone with volcanic grit, about 270 million years old, hot and bare, the Kamptal's Riesling summit; Ried Zöbinger Heiligenstein stands on the labels of the valley's best houses.

places.name: Kammern
places.note: Beneath the Heiligenstein: the Lamm, loess and clay at the hill's foot, is the Kamptal's finest Grüner Veltliner site, and the Grub, Renner and Gaisberg rise beside it.

places.name: Gobelsburg
places.note: The village and its castle estate, which has belonged to the Cistercian abbey of Zwettl since 1740, with vineyards in the Heiligenstein, Lamm, Renner and Grub.

places.name: Traisental
places.note: The smallest Danube region, up the Traisen river south of Krems: limestone conglomerate soils unusual for Austria, Traisental DAC since the 2006 vintage for Grüner Veltliner and Riesling.

places.name: Wagram
places.note: The loess ridge above the Danube's north bank east of the Kamptal, Wagram DAC since the 2021 vintage: deep loess Grüner Veltliner and the native Roter Veltliner.

places.name: Carnuntum
places.note: East of Vienna south of the Danube, Roman ruins and warm Pannonian slopes: Carnuntum DAC since the 2019 vintage for Zweigelt and Blaufränkisch reds and for Chardonnay, Weissburgunder and Grüner Veltliner whites; the Spitzerberg is its Blaufränkisch cru.

places.name: Thermenregion
places.note: South of Vienna around the spa towns of Baden and Bad Vöslau, Thermenregion DAC since 2023: Rotgipfler and Zierfandler at Gumpoldskirchen, Pinot Noir and St. Laurent at Tattendorf.

producers.name: Franz Hirtzberger
producers.why: Spitz; the Singerriedel Riesling and Honivogl Grüner Veltliner Smaragd are the Wachau's richest, most honeyed reference wines.

producers.name: Emmerich Knoll
producers.why: Unterloiben; Loibenberg and Schütt Smaragd behind the baroque saint on the label, wines of unusual longevity.

producers.name: F.X. Pichler
producers.why: Oberloiben; Kellerberg and Steinertal Riesling of concentration and polish, the Wachau's most famous name abroad.

producers.name: Weingut Prager
producers.why: Weissenkirchen; a co-founder of the Vinea Wachau in 1983 and a pioneer of dry Wachau Riesling from the Achleiten and Klaus.

producers.name: Nikolaihof
producers.why: Mautern; an ancient estate on Roman foundations, biodynamic since 1971, with Riesling and Grüner Veltliner aged for years in old casks.

producers.name: Domäne Wachau
producers.why: Dürnstein; the cooperative that farms a large share of the terraces and bottles the Kellerberg and Achleiten at every level from Federspiel to Smaragd.

producers.name: Alzinger
producers.why: Unterloiben; precise, taut Riesling from the Steinertal and Loibenberg, among the most finely drawn in the gorge.

producers.name: Jamek
producers.why: Joching; the house that showed dry Wachau Riesling to the world in the 1950s, with the Klaus as its flag.

producers.name: Bründlmayer
producers.why: Langenlois; the Kamptal's leading estate, Zöbinger Heiligenstein Riesling, Lamm Grüner Veltliner, old vine and terrace cuvées and a serious traditional method Sekt.

producers.name: Loimer
producers.why: Langenlois; biodynamic Grüner Veltliner and Riesling from the Käferberg and Steinmassl, and an entry cuvée that reaches many restaurant lists.

producers.name: Schloss Gobelsburg
producers.why: Gobelsburg; the Cistercian castle estate, Heiligenstein and Lamm, with a tradition line of wines made in old wooden casks moved on wheels.

producers.name: Hirsch
producers.why: Kammern; Heiligenstein, Lamm and Gaisberg, an early mover to screwcap and organic farming in the Kamptal.

producers.name: Weingut Nigl
producers.why: Senftenberg; the Kremstal's benchmark for steely Riesling and Grüner Veltliner from the Pellingen and Piri terraces.

producers.name: Salomon Undhof
producers.why: Stein; Riesling from the Pfaffenberg and Kögl at the Kremstal's rockiest edge, one of Austria's oldest family estates.

exam: Place the three regions on the Danube: the Wachau gorge from Melk to Krems, the Kremstal around Krems, the Kamptal up the Kamp at Langenlois.
Recite the Vinea Wachau scale with its alcohol lines: Steinfeder to 11.5%, Federspiel 11.5 to 12.5%, Smaragd from 12.5%, and what each name means.
Know that the Kamptal, Kremstal and Traisental DACs name Grüner Veltliner and Riesling only, and the Wachau DAC the same two at Riedenwein level.
Match soil to grape: Riesling on primary rock (gneiss), Grüner Veltliner on loess.
Name the Heiligenstein, the Kellerberg, the Achleiten, the Loibenberg and the Lamm and say which grape each is famous for.
Give the DAC years: Traisental 2006, Kremstal 2007, Kamptal 2008, Wachau 2020, Wagram 2021.
Know the Wachau DAC's hand harvest rule and its tiers of 17, 9 and 2 grapes.
traps: Smaragd, Federspiel and Steinfeder are the Vinea Wachau's private scale, measured in alcohol because the wines are dry; they are not Prädikat levels and not used in the Kamptal or Kremstal.
The Wachau DAC did not replace the Vinea Wachau categories: a label may carry Wachau DAC and Smaragd together.
Stein belongs to the Kremstal although its terraces are continuous with the Wachau's; the gorge ends at the Krems town line.
The Heiligenstein is sandstone and volcanic grit, not gneiss, and not loess; the Lamm at its foot is the loess and clay Grüner Veltliner site.
Kremstal DAC came before Kamptal DAC (2007 then 2008), both after Traisental (2006) and long after the Weinviertel (2002).
Reserve in these DACs means at least 13% alcohol and a dry wine, not a sweet or an oaked one.

cards.f: The Vinea Wachau scale, with its alcohol lines
cards.b: Steinfeder, at most 11.5% (a feathery grass); Federspiel, 11.5 to 12.5% (a falconer's lure); Smaragd, from 12.5% (the emerald lizard). Dry wines, a growers' scale from 1983, not law.
Gebietswein, 17 grapes; Ortswein, 9 grapes from 22 villages; Riedenwein, Grüner Veltliner and Riesling only. Hand harvest at every tier; from the 2020 vintage.

cards.f: Grüner on loess, Riesling on rock: why
cards.b: Loess holds water and lime and feeds the vigorous Grüner Veltliner; thin gneiss terraces starve and warm the vine, which suits late ripening Riesling.

cards.f: Kamptal, Kremstal, Traisental DAC: grapes and years
cards.b: Grüner Veltliner and Riesling only. Traisental 2006, Kremstal 2007, Kamptal 2008. Klassik and Reserve (13% minimum), now also Gebietswein, Ortswein and Riedenwein.
The Kamptal's great hill above Zöbing: Permian sandstone with volcanic grit, about 270 million years old. Riesling. The Lamm at its foot is loess and clay for Grüner Veltliner.
Spitz, Weissenkirchen (with Joching and Wösendorf), Dürnstein, Loiben; Mautern faces them on the south bank. Krems and Stein begin the Kremstal.
Singerriedel and Honivogl (Spitz), Achleiten and Klaus (Weissenkirchen), Kellerberg (Dürnstein), Loibenberg and Schütt (Loiben), Pfaffenberg (Stein), Heiligenstein (Zöbing), Lamm (Kammern).

cards.f: Niederösterreich's other regions and their DAC years
cards.b: Wagram 2021 (Roter Veltliner on loess), Carnuntum 2019 (Zweigelt and Blaufränkisch), Thermenregion 2023 (Rotgipfler, Zierfandler, Pinot Noir, St. Laurent).

questions.q: Which Vinea Wachau category carries at least 12.5% alcohol?
questions.exp: Smaragd, named for the emerald lizard of the terraces, starts at 12.5%; Federspiel runs 11.5 to 12.5% and Steinfeder stops at 11.5%. Klassik is a Kamptal and Kremstal DAC term.

questions.q: Which grape is the Zöbinger Heiligenstein famous for?
questions.exp: The Heiligenstein's hot Permian sandstone is the Kamptal's Riesling summit; the Lamm at its foot, on loess and clay, is the Grüner Veltliner site.

questions.q: On which soil is Riesling planted in the Wachau?
questions.exp: Riesling takes the thin, water poor primary rock terraces of gneiss and amphibolite; Grüner Veltliner takes the deep loess beside them. Limestone marks the Traisental and basalt the Styrian Vulkanland.

questions.q: Which two grapes may be labelled as Kamptal DAC?
questions.exp: Kamptal DAC, like Kremstal and Traisental, is reserved for Grüner Veltliner and Riesling, dry; any other grape from the valley is sold as Niederösterreich Qualitätswein.

questions.q: From which vintage has the Wachau been a DAC?
questions.exp: The Wachau DAC ordinance was issued in 2020 for that vintage; Kremstal came in 2007, Kamptal in 2008 and Carnuntum in 2019.

questions.q: Which two towns mark the ends of the Wachau along the Danube?
questions.exp: The Wachau is the gorge between Melk upstream and Krems downstream; Krems itself and Stein belong to the Kremstal, and Tulln lies in the Wagram region further east.

questions.q: Which village is the Kellerberg vineyard in?
questions.exp: The Kellerberg rises above Dürnstein; Spitz has the Singerriedel, Weissenkirchen the Achleiten, and Loiben the Loibenberg and Schütt.

questions.q: Which tier of the Wachau DAC is limited to Grüner Veltliner and Riesling?
questions.exp: The Wachau DAC narrows from 17 grapes at Gebietswein and 9 at Ortswein to Grüner Veltliner and Riesling alone for a Riedenwein, hand picked and never chaptalised. Reserve is a rung of the Kamptal and Kremstal DACs, not the Wachau's.

regions.name: Wien (Vienna)
regions.summary: Vienna is the only capital city with a serious commercial vineyard inside its limits, and its wine is drunk in the Heuriger taverns where it grows. The vines sit on the city's northern and southern edges: the Nussberg and the Heurigen villages of the 19th district on the right bank of the Danube, the Bisamberg across the river, and Mauer and Oberlaa in the south. The signature is Wiener Gemischter Satz, a field blend of at least three white grapes planted, picked and fermented together, a DAC since the 2013 vintage. Grüner Veltliner, Riesling and Weissburgunder are bottled alone too, with a little Zweigelt. Everything is dry, fresh and meant for the table.

terroir.climate: Continental with the Pannonian pull of the east: warm summers, cold winters, dry air, and the city's own warmth lifting the night temperatures a degree or two. The slopes above the Danube catch the breeze along the river; the southern districts are a little warmer and drier. Ripening is reliable and botrytis rare, so the harvest comes in dry and the wines keep their acidity.
terroir.soils: The Nussberg and the Döbling hills are limestone and calcareous sandstone of the Vienna Woods' foothills, with shell limestone and marl in places; the Bisamberg is lime rich loess over flysch sandstone; Mauer and the south lie on brown earth, gravel and loess. The limestone gives the Gemischter Satz its saline, chalky edge; the loess gives Grüner Veltliner its breadth.
terroir.topography: Two bands of hills at the city's edge. In the north the Vienna Woods drop towards the Danube in the Nussberg, Kahlenberg and the villages of Grinzing, Sievering and Neustift am Walde; across the river the Bisamberg rises over Stammersdorf and Strebersdorf. In the south the Maurer Berg and the Laaer Berg carry the vines of Mauer and Oberlaa. Most slopes face south and east and sit between about 200 and 400 metres.
terroir.water: The Danube divides the city's vineyards: the right bank hills look over it from the Nussberg, the Bisamberg from the left. It moderates the frost and reflects light onto the lower slopes.

grapes.name: Grüner Veltliner
grapes.styles: The most planted grape of the city, bottled alone from the Bisamberg's loess and as the backbone of most Gemischter Satz: peppery, fresh, drunk young at the Heuriger.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: The Nussberg's finest single varietal, dry and stony on limestone, and a usual partner in the field blends.

grapes.name: Pinot Blanc
grapes.styles: Weissburgunder: rounds the Gemischter Satz and stands alone as a soft, creamy white.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Grown in the field blends and alone, mostly unoaked and lean, with some barrel aged bottlings from the Nussberg.

grapes.name: Neuburger
grapes.styles: An old Vienna grape, nutty and gentle, a traditional strand of the field blends.

grapes.name: Rotgipfler
grapes.styles: Borrowed from the Thermenregion to the south; it and Zierfandler add honeyed weight to Gemischter Satz from the southern vineyards.

grapes.name: Zierfandler
grapes.styles: Spicy and long lived; appears as a strand in the old mixed plantings of Mauer and the Nussberg.

grapes.name: Zweigelt
grapes.styles: The city's red for the Heuriger, light and cherried; a few serious bottlings from the Bisamberg and the south.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Blauburgunder in small plots, silky and light, part of the modern estates' ranges.

wines.note: A field blend of at least three white grapes grown together: fresh, dry, apple and white flowers with a saline edge, and no one grape showing. Without a vineyard name it is light, at most 12.5% alcohol; with a Ried or village name it is fuller and may be riper. Serve cool with schnitzel, cold cuts and the Heuriger buffet.
Dry, lime and stone, from the limestone slope above Nussdorf; the city's most age worthy white.
Peppery and quick, the house pour of the Heuriger, often from the Bisamberg's loess; by the glass it carries fried food and sausages.
The current vintage, young and simple, poured by the quarter litre at a grower's own tavern under a pine bough that signals it is open; the word means this year's.
Fermenting grape must, cloudy, sweet and lightly fizzy, sold for a few autumn weeks only and never bottled for keeping.

made.viticulture: The field blend is the farming choice that defines Vienna. For a Wiener Gemischter Satz DAC the vineyard must be registered as a mixed planting: at least three white Qualitätswein grapes grown together in one Vienna vineyard, the largest taking no more than half the vines and the third largest at least a tenth, all picked together and pressed together. The old mixed vineyards of the Nussberg and Mauer carry a dozen or more varieties side by side; new plantings copy the pattern on purpose. Grapes are picked by hand on the slopes, where plots are small and hemmed in by houses and woods. Pressure on the land is the city's hazard: vineyard is protected by municipal rule, and the City of Vienna farms its own estate at Cobenzl above Grinzing to keep the slopes in vine. Spring frost is rare on the hills and botrytis uncommon in the dry air; birds and wild boar from the Vienna Woods take their share. Vines are wire trained and most estates work organically or near it.
made.winemaking: Gemischter Satz is made as one wine from the start: the grapes arrive together, go through the press together and ferment together, usually cool in stainless steel, so that no variety can be separated out afterwards. That is the legal and the stylistic point, and it is what separates a field blend from a cuvée assembled in the cellar. The DAC wine without a vineyard name must be dry and must not show a dominant oak note; a bottling with a Ried or village name needs at least 12.5% alcohol and may carry a little more sugar and a touch of cask. Single varietals follow the Austrian norm, dry and reductive with a few months on fine lees. Heuriger wine is bottled or kegged within months of the harvest and sold in the grower's own tavern, a right the growers have held since the Josephinian decree of 1784. Sturm is must stopped nowhere, sold mid ferment.

law.classification: Wien is both one of Austria's four generic wine growing regions and a specific region with its own DAC. Wiener Gemischter Satz DAC, from the 2013 vintage, protects the field blend alone: at least three white Qualitätswein grapes from one registered Vienna vineyard, co planted and co harvested, the largest share at most 50% and the third at least 10%. The plain DAC is dry and at most 12.5% alcohol with no dominant wood; a wine naming a Ried or a village must reach 12.5% and need not be dry. Every other Vienna wine, varietal or red, is Wien Qualitätswein under the national ladder. The Heuriger is governed by a Vienna statute: a grower may sell only his own wine, from his own vineyards, in his own premises, for a set number of days.
tiers: Wiener Gemischter Satz DAC
The field blend without a vineyard name: dry, at most 12.5% alcohol, no dominant oak.
Wiener Gemischter Satz DAC with Ried or village
The same blend from a named site or village: at least 12.5% alcohol, dryness not required, a fuller, longer lived wine.
Wien Qualitätswein
Every other wine of the city: Grüner Veltliner, Riesling, Weissburgunder, Zweigelt and the rest, under the national rules.
labels: Mixed planting: a field blend grown, picked and fermented together; outside Vienna the term may be used without the DAC.
This year's wine, and the grower's tavern that sells it; the tavern hangs a pine bough and the word ausg'steckt when open.
The legal name of the grower's tavern, in Vienna and across Austria.
A group of leading city estates formed in 2006 to promote Wiener Gemischter Satz as a fine wine.

places.name: Nussberg
places.note: The great south facing slope above Nussdorf and Heiligenstadt in the 19th district, limestone and sandstone looking over the Danube: Vienna's grand cru for Riesling and for the most serious Gemischter Satz, with Rieden such as Preussen and Ulm.

places.name: Grinzing, Sievering and Neustift am Walde
places.note: The Heurigen villages of the Vienna Woods' foothills in the 19th district: small plots between the houses, Gemischter Satz and Grüner Veltliner drunk in the taverns a few steps from the vines; the City of Vienna's own Cobenzl estate sits above Grinzing.

places.name: Bisamberg
places.note: The hill on the left bank of the Danube over Stammersdorf and Strebersdorf in the 21st district, loess over limestone and flysch: broad Grüner Veltliner, Weissburgunder and Riesling, and the city's largest block of vines; it continues into the Weinviertel beyond the city line.

places.name: Mauer
places.note: The southern vineyards of the 23rd district on the Maurer Berg at the foot of the Vienna Woods, brown earth and limestone, old mixed plantings with Zierfandler and Rotgipfler strands, and a quieter Heuriger scene.

places.name: Oberlaa
places.note: The Laaer Berg in the 10th district, the city's south eastern slope on loess and gravel, warmer and drier, with Grüner Veltliner and reds.

producers.name: Weingut Wieninger
producers.why: Stammersdorf and the Nussberg; the house that made Wiener Gemischter Satz a fine wine again and led the push for its DAC.

producers.name: Mayer am Pfarrplatz
producers.why: Heiligenstadt; Nussberg Riesling and Gemischter Satz from the house where Beethoven lodged in 1817, with a famous Heuriger.

producers.name: Weingut Cobenzl
producers.why: Grinzing; the estate owned by the City of Vienna, keeping the slopes above Grinzing in vine and showing the city's field blends at an honest price.

producers.name: Christ
producers.why: Jedlersdorf on the Bisamberg; Gemischter Satz and single varietals from the left bank, with a large and well known Heuriger.

producers.name: Zahel
producers.why: Mauer; the leading estate of the southern vineyards, with old mixed plantings on the Maurer Berg.

producers.name: Fuhrgassl-Huber
producers.why: Neustift am Walde; a classic Heuriger house of the 19th district whose Gemischter Satz reaches export lists.

exam: Define Wiener Gemischter Satz DAC: at least three white grapes co planted in one Vienna vineyard, largest share at most 50%, third largest at least 10%, co harvested and co fermented, from the 2013 vintage.
Tell a field blend from a cellar blend and explain why the law cares.
Place the Nussberg (right bank, Döbling) and the Bisamberg (left bank) on the Danube.
Know the alcohol line that separates the plain DAC (at most 12.5%) from a Ried or village bottling (at least 12.5%).
Explain the Heuriger and the pine bough, and the 1784 decree that created the trade.
Name Vienna as both a generic region and a specific DAC region, the only capital with commercial vineyard inside its limits.
traps: Gemischter Satz is grown together and fermented together; a Grüner Veltliner blended with Riesling in the tank is a cuvée, not a Gemischter Satz.
The DAC covers only the field blend; a Vienna Riesling is Wien Qualitätswein, not Wiener Gemischter Satz DAC.
The plain DAC has a maximum alcohol (12.5%), not a minimum; the Ried and village wines flip it to a minimum of 12.5%.
Heuriger means this year's wine as well as the tavern; it is not a place name and not a grape.
The Bisamberg is across the Danube from the Nussberg and runs on into the Weinviertel; the Nussberg is in the city's 19th district.
Sturm is unfinished wine sold mid ferment, not a sparkling wine and not a Prädikat.

cards.f: Wiener Gemischter Satz DAC: the rule
cards.b: At least three white Qualitätswein grapes co planted in one Vienna vineyard, picked and fermented together; largest share at most 50%, third largest at least 10%. DAC from the 2013 vintage.

cards.f: Plain DAC versus Ried or village DAC
cards.b: Plain: dry, at most 12.5% alcohol, no dominant oak. With a Ried or village name: at least 12.5% alcohol, need not be dry.
Nussberg and the Döbling villages (Grinzing, Sievering, Neustift) on the right bank; Bisamberg over Stammersdorf on the left; Mauer and Oberlaa in the south.
A field blend grows, is picked and ferments as one wine; a cuvée is assembled in the cellar from separately made wines. Only the first may be called Gemischter Satz.
A grower's tavern selling only its own wine, open on set days under a pine bough; also the current year's wine. Right granted by Joseph II's decree of 1784.

cards.f: Vienna's soils and what they give
cards.b: Limestone and calcareous sandstone on the Nussberg (saline Riesling and Gemischter Satz); loess over limestone on the Bisamberg (broad Grüner Veltliner); brown earth and gravel in the south.
Grape must caught mid fermentation: cloudy, sweet, faintly fizzy, drunk within days in autumn. Not a wine category and not for ageing.

questions.q: How many white grape varieties, at the least, must a Wiener Gemischter Satz DAC contain?
questions.exp: The DAC asks for at least three white Qualitätswein grapes co planted in one Vienna vineyard, with the largest at most half and the third largest at least a tenth of the planting.

questions.q: What is the maximum alcohol of a Wiener Gemischter Satz DAC that names no vineyard or village?
questions.exp: The plain DAC is dry and capped at 12.5% alcohol; a bottling with a Ried or village name reverses the rule and must reach at least 12.5%.

questions.q: On which bank of the Danube does the Nussberg lie?
opts: The right bank, in the 19th district
The left bank, in the 21st district
The right bank, in the 23rd district
The left bank, in the 22nd district
questions.exp: The Nussberg rises over Nussdorf and Heiligenstadt in Döbling, the 19th district, on the right bank; the Bisamberg faces it from the left bank in the 21st.

questions.q: From which vintage has Wiener Gemischter Satz been a DAC?
questions.exp: Wiener Gemischter Satz DAC was created for the 2013 vintage; 2008 was the Kamptal's DAC year and 2016 the vintage from which Ried became compulsory before vineyard names.

questions.q: What is the Austrian name for partly fermented grape must sold in autumn?
questions.exp: Sturm is cloudy, sweet, fizzy must caught mid ferment and sold for a few weeks; it is drunk fresh and never kept.

questions.q: Under Vienna's Heuriger rule, whose wine may a Heuriger sell?
opts: Any wine bought from a merchant
questions.exp: A Heuriger is a grower's own tavern: Vienna's statute, rooted in Joseph II's decree of 1784, lets it sell only wine from its own vineyards, on its own premises, for a set number of days each year, under the pine bough that shows it is open.

questions.q: Which hill carries Vienna's vineyards on the left bank of the Danube?
questions.exp: The Bisamberg rises over Stammersdorf and Strebersdorf on the left bank; the Nussberg and Kahlenberg are on the right bank and the Laaer Berg is in the city's south.

regions.name: Weinviertel
regions.summary: The Weinviertel, the wine quarter, is the largest wine region in Austria, a rolling plateau of loess and limestone that fills the north east of Niederösterreich between the Manhartsberg, the Danube and the Czech and Slovak borders. It is Grüner Veltliner's homeland and the birthplace of the DAC: Weinviertel DAC, created in 2002 for that vintage, was Austria's first and is reserved for peppery Grüner Veltliner alone, Klassik and, since 2009, Reserve. Retz, Poysdorf, Falkenstein and Wolkersdorf are the names to hold, Poysdorf as the Sekt town. The wines are dry, fresh, modestly priced and marked by the local word Pfefferl, the little pepper.

terroir.climate: Dry continental: this is among the driest parts of Austria, with cold winters, warm summers and little rain, open to Pannonian warmth from the east and to cold north winds off the Czech hills. Frost is the spring hazard on the open plateau and drought the summer one. The north around Poysdorf and Falkenstein is cooler and later, a source of Eiswein; the south near Vienna is warmer; the west around Retz, under the Manhartsberg, is the driest and sunniest corner.
terroir.soils: Loess above all, deep and lime rich, which gives Grüner Veltliner its breadth and keeps it from drought. Limestone outcrops at Falkenstein and Staatz, where Jurassic klippen break the surface; granite and gneiss of the Bohemian Massif around Retz and Röschitz in the west; sand, gravel and clay marls of the old Tertiary sea in the east around Matzen and Zistersdorf.
terroir.topography: A plateau of low hills and wide valleys between 200 and 400 metres, nothing steep, worked by machine on gentle south and south east slopes. The Manhartsberg ridge walls it off from the Kamptal in the west; the Bisamberg and the Danube bound it in the south; the March valley lies to the east. Villages are strung with Kellergassen, lanes of press houses and cellars dug into the loess.
terroir.water: No river shapes it the way the Danube shapes the Wachau. The Pulkau runs through the west, the Zaya through the north east, and the March marks the Slovak border; the Danube and the Bisamberg close the southern edge.

grapes.name: Grüner Veltliner
grapes.styles: About half the vineyard and the only grape of the DAC: green apple, white pepper and a snap of radish, light and spritzy as Klassik, deeper and more honeyed as Reserve from the limestone and the best loess.

grapes.name: Welschriesling
grapes.styles: Crisp, neutral, high in acid: the second white, a base for Sekt at Poysdorf and for Heuriger wine.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: A small share on the granite around Retz and the limestone of Falkenstein, dry and firm.

grapes.name: Pinot Blanc
grapes.styles: Weissburgunder for softer whites and for Sekt bases.

grapes.name: Zweigelt
grapes.styles: The main red, light and cherried in the north, more serious at Mailberg and in the south around Wolkersdorf.

grapes.name: Blaufränkisch
grapes.styles: A little in the warmer south and in the Mailberg valley, lighter than Burgenland's.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Blauburgunder in the Mailberg valley and the south, and a base for Sekt.

wines.note: Grüner Veltliner at its freshest: at least 12% alcohol, dry, green apple and white pepper, no oak, no botrytis. The glass pour for schnitzel, fried chicken, oysters and anything with a squeeze of lemon.
The riper rung from the 2009 vintage: at least 13% alcohol, dry, with a little weight from cask or ripe fruit allowed, released later and built to sit with roast pork and veal.
Sparkling from the town long regarded as Austria's Sekt capital, where Welschriesling and Grüner Veltliner make crisp base wines for the Sekt Austria tiers.
From the cold north around Poysdorf: Grüner Veltliner or Welschriesling frozen on the vine at 25° KMW, taut and clean, a glass with fruit tarts.
Light, bright, cherry fruited red from the loess, served slightly cool; the Mailberg valley makes the fuller versions.

made.viticulture: This is machine country: wide rows on gentle loess slopes, wire trained vines on high cordons, mechanical harvesting for the Klassik wines and hand picking reserved for the Reserve and the single Rieden. The region's size makes it Austria's volume engine and its cooperative and merchant base, and yields are higher than on the Danube terraces. Drought is the constant pressure on the dry plateau, and the loess's water holding is what makes Grüner Veltliner possible without irrigation in most years; spring frost on the open ground and hail in summer are the other hazards. Grüner Veltliner is picked early for the Klassik style, while the sugars are moderate and the pepper is sharp, and later for the Reserve. In the cold north growers leave rows of Grüner Veltliner or Welschriesling for Eiswein, picking frozen bunches in the dark before dawn. Vineyards sit beside the Kellergassen, the cellar lanes, where each family's press house opens onto the road and the cellars run back into the loess. Organic farming has grown but the region remains conventional at its base.
made.winemaking: The Klassik style is the simplest Austrian winemaking and the most widely copied: clean must, cool fermentation in stainless steel, a few months on fine lees and early bottling, often under screwcap, with a little carbon dioxide left in for the Pfefferl snap. The DAC rules keep it so: dry, at least 12% alcohol, no obvious wood, no botrytis character, fresh and peppery or it fails the tasting panel. The Reserve, from the 2009 vintage, allows at least 13% alcohol, a delicate oak or botrytis note and a later release, which brings large old casks and longer lees ageing into play at the better estates. Sekt at Poysdorf is both tank and traditional method, the latter under the Sekt Austria pyramid's Reserve and Grosse Reserve rules. Eiswein is pressed frozen and fermented slowly to a sweet, light wine.

law.classification: The Weinviertel is a specific wine growing region of Niederösterreich and the home of Austria's first DAC. Weinviertel DAC, created in 2002 for that vintage, is reserved for dry Grüner Veltliner that tastes of the region: fruity, spicy and peppery, with at least 12% alcohol and no wood or botrytis character, approved by a tasting panel. Weinviertel DAC Reserve was added with the 2009 vintage for riper wines of at least 13% alcohol, dry, where a subtle wood or botrytis note is allowed and the release comes later. Every other wine of the region, including Grüner Veltliner that fails the panel, is sold as Niederösterreich Qualitätswein, and single vineyards carry the word Ried.
tiers: Weinviertel DAC
Grüner Veltliner only, dry, at least 12% alcohol, fresh and peppery, no obvious oak or botrytis.
Weinviertel DAC Reserve
Grüner Veltliner only, dry, at least 13% alcohol, a delicate wood or botrytis note allowed, released later; from the 2009 vintage.
Niederösterreich Qualitätswein
Every other wine of the Weinviertel: Welschriesling, Riesling, Zweigelt and the rest, or Grüner Veltliner outside the DAC style.
labels: The little pepper: the local word for the white pepper tell of Weinviertel Grüner Veltliner.
A cellar lane: a street of press houses with cellars dug into the loess behind them, a feature of nearly every Weinviertel village.
The western Weinviertel around Retz, the driest corner, on granite and loess.
The national sparkling pyramid; Poysdorf is the Weinviertel's Sekt town.

places.name: Retz and the western Weinviertel
places.note: Under the Manhartsberg against the Czech border: Retz with its famous cellar labyrinth beneath the town, Röschitz, Pulkau and Haugsdorf on granite, gneiss and loess, the driest and sunniest corner, Grüner Veltliner and a little Riesling.

places.name: Mailberg
places.note: A sheltered basin south east of Retz, a warm pocket that makes the Weinviertel's best reds, Zweigelt and Blaufränkisch beside the Grüner Veltliner; the Knights of Malta have held an estate here since the twelfth century.

places.name: Poysdorf
places.note: The northern Weinviertel's wine town, cool and late, long regarded as Austria's Sekt capital: Welschriesling and Grüner Veltliner for sparkling bases, Eiswein in cold years, and the Weinviertel DAC Reserve style from its loess slopes.

places.name: Falkenstein
places.note: Beneath a ruined castle on a Jurassic limestone cliff in the north, with Herrnbaumgarten and Staatz nearby: Grüner Veltliner with a chalky grip, among the region's most structured, and a classic Kellergasse.

places.name: Wolkersdorf and the southern Weinviertel
places.note: The warmest band, from the Bisamberg's northern slopes past Wolkersdorf and Stetten towards the Danube: riper Grüner Veltliner Reserve, Riesling on the Bisamberg's limestone and more red than the north.

places.name: Matzen and the eastern Weinviertel
places.note: Towards the March valley and the Slovak border, the Marchfeld's edge: sand, gravel and marl, Zistersdorf and Hohenruppersdorf, Grüner Veltliner and Welschriesling for the cooperatives and Heuriger trade.

producers.name: Pfaffl
producers.why: Stetten, on the Bisamberg's northern side; the southern Weinviertel's leading estate, with a wide range of Grüner Veltliner from Klassik to Reserve and reds beside it.

producers.name: Ebner-Ebenauer
producers.why: Poysdorf; small, serious single vineyard Grüner Veltliner and traditional method Sekt from the north.

producers.name: Zull
producers.why: Schrattenthal near Retz; dry, precise Grüner Veltliner and Riesling from the granite and loess of the far west.

producers.name: Gruber Röschitz
producers.why: Röschitz; a family estate of the Retzer Land, Weinviertel DAC Grüner Veltliner with the Pfefferl at a fair price.

producers.name: Weinrieder
producers.why: Kleinhadersdorf by Poysdorf; the specialist of the cold north, known for Eiswein and Beerenauslese beside its dry Grüner Veltliner.

producers.name: Setzer
producers.why: Hohenwarth; Grüner Veltliner from old vines on loess and limestone, a reference for the DAC Reserve.

exam: Know the Weinviertel as Austria's largest region, in the north east of Niederösterreich, north of Vienna and the Danube.
Give the first DAC: Weinviertel, 2002 vintage, Grüner Veltliner only, dry, at least 12% alcohol, peppery.
Know the Reserve rung: from 2009, at least 13%, dry, a little wood or botrytis allowed.
Hold the soils: loess above all, limestone at Falkenstein, granite and gneiss at Retz.
Name Poysdorf as the Sekt town and Retz for its cellars.
Say Pfefferl and explain it as the white pepper tell of Grüner Veltliner.
traps: The Weinviertel DAC was the first, not the Wachau's: 2002 for the Weinviertel, 2020 for the Wachau.
Weinviertel DAC means Grüner Veltliner and nothing else; a Weinviertel Riesling is Niederösterreich Qualitätswein.
The DAC's 12% is a minimum, and the wine must be dry; it is not a cap like Vienna's plain Gemischter Satz.
The Weinviertel lies north of the Danube and of Vienna; Carnuntum and the Thermenregion lie east and south of the city.
Loess is the soil of the Weinviertel and of the Kremstal's east, not of the Wachau's terraces, which are gneiss.
Kellergassen are cellar lanes in the villages, not vineyards and not a classification.

cards.b: Grüner Veltliner only, dry, at least 12% alcohol, fresh and peppery with no obvious oak or botrytis; Austria's first DAC, created in 2002 for that vintage.
From the 2009 vintage: Grüner Veltliner, dry, at least 13% alcohol, a delicate wood or botrytis note allowed, released later.
North east Niederösterreich: north of Vienna and the Danube, Manhartsberg in the west, Czech border north, March river and Slovakia east. Austria's largest region.
Granite and gneiss at Retz; loess nearly everywhere; Jurassic limestone klippen at Falkenstein and Staatz; sand, gravel and marl towards the March.
Retz (west, cellars), Mailberg (reds), Poysdorf (north, Sekt, Eiswein), Falkenstein (limestone), Wolkersdorf and Stetten (warm south by the Bisamberg).
The little pepper: the Weinviertel's word for the white pepper and radish bite of its Grüner Veltliner, the DAC's required character.
A lane of press houses with cellars tunnelled into the loess behind, found in most Weinviertel villages; a cultural feature, not a vineyard rank.

questions.q: Which was the first Austrian region to receive a DAC?
questions.exp: Weinviertel DAC was created in 2002 for that vintage; Mittelburgenland followed in 2005, Kamptal in 2008 and the Wachau only in 2020.

questions.q: Which grape alone may be labelled Weinviertel DAC?
questions.exp: The Weinviertel DAC protects dry, peppery Grüner Veltliner and no other grape; Welschriesling, Riesling and Zweigelt from the region are Niederösterreich Qualitätswein.

questions.q: What is the minimum alcohol of a Weinviertel DAC Reserve?
questions.exp: The Reserve, added with the 2009 vintage, asks at least 13% alcohol and a dry wine, where the Klassik DAC asks 12%.

questions.q: What does the Weinviertel word Pfefferl describe?
accept: The white pepper note of Grüner Veltliner
questions.ans: The white pepper note of Grüner Veltliner
questions.exp: Pfefferl, the little pepper, is the local name for the white pepper and radish bite that the DAC requires of the region's Grüner Veltliner.

questions.q: Which soil covers most of the Weinviertel's vineyard?
questions.exp: Deep, lime rich loess underlies most of the plateau and feeds Grüner Veltliner; gneiss is the Wachau's terrace rock, slate the Mosel's, basalt the Styrian Vulkanland's.

questions.q: Which Weinviertel town is regarded as Austria's Sekt capital?
questions.exp: Poysdorf in the cool north has long made sparkling base wine from Welschriesling and Grüner Veltliner; Retz is known for its cellars, Mailberg for reds and Falkenstein for limestone.

questions.q: In which direction from Vienna does the Weinviertel lie?
questions.exp: The Weinviertel fills the north east of Niederösterreich north of Vienna and the Danube; the Thermenregion lies south of the city, Carnuntum east and the Wagram and Danube regions west.
