regions.name: Burgenland
regions.summary: Burgenland is the long, thin federal state down Austria's eastern border with Hungary, and the country's red and sweet wine heartland. The Neusiedlersee, a vast steppe lake barely a metre or two deep, sits at its northern end: the Seewinkel on its east shore makes botrytis sweet wines and Zweigelt reds, the Leithaberg on the west shore makes mineral whites and Blaufränkisch on limestone and schist, and the free town of Rust makes Ruster Ausbruch. South of the lake the Rosalia hills, then Mittelburgenland, the Blaufränkisch country, then the Eisenberg in the far south on iron rich slate. Six DACs cover it, five of them naming Blaufränkisch or Zweigelt. The climate is Pannonian, Austria's warmest.

terroir.climate: Pannonian: hot, dry summers, cold winters and more sunshine than anywhere else in Austria, with the east wind off the Hungarian plain. Around the lake the autumn brings morning mists that lift by midday, the conditions botrytis needs, so noble rot comes nearly every year to the Seewinkel. Mittelburgenland is sheltered from the west by hills and open to the plain, warm enough to ripen Blaufränkisch fully; the Eisenberg in the south is a touch cooler and wetter, with the Alps' last foothills to the west.
terroir.soils: Varied, and the exam asks for the pattern: sand, gravel, loam and black earth on the Seewinkel's flats, with salt pans between the vines; Leitha limestone and mica schist on the Leithaberg's slopes; deep, heavy clay and loam in Mittelburgenland that gives Blaufränkisch its weight; green schist, slate and iron rich loam at the Eisenberg that give it its mineral bite. Rust's slopes are limestone and schist, its lakeside flats sand and loam.
terroir.topography: The north is a plain around the lake, with the Leitha range rising gently on the west shore to under 500 metres and the Seewinkel flat as a table on the east. The Rosalia hills and the Ödenburg range separate it from Mittelburgenland, a basin of low hills open to Hungary. The south narrows to a strip of hills along the Pinka valley, where the Eisenberg and the Csaterberg stand as the last vineyards before the border.
terroir.water: The Neusiedlersee is the engine: about 36 kilometres long, one to two metres deep, ringed by reeds, warming fast in spring and holding warmth into autumn, breeding the mists that bring botrytis. It has no natural outflow. The Leitha river gives the Leithaberg its name; the Pinka runs past the Eisenberg.

grapes.name: Blaufränkisch
grapes.styles: The serious red of the state: dark cherry, blackberry, black pepper, iron and bright acidity with firm tannin; weighty from Mittelburgenland's clay, mineral and fine from the Leithaberg's schist and limestone, savoury and taut from the Eisenberg's slate.

grapes.name: Zweigelt
grapes.styles: The most planted grape of the Seewinkel and of Burgenland as a whole: juicy sour cherry and soft tannin for drinking young, deeper and cask aged as Neusiedlersee DAC Reserve, and a partner in the Pannonian blends.

grapes.name: Welschriesling
grapes.styles: The great botrytis grape of the Seewinkel, thin skinned and acid, the backbone of Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese and a strand of Ruster Ausbruch; dry it is a light spritzy white.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Rich, oak aged dry whites on the Leithaberg and the Seewinkel, and the other half of the lake's classic sweet cuvées with Welschriesling.

grapes.name: Pinot Blanc
grapes.styles: Weissburgunder: one of the Leithaberg DAC's four white grapes, dry, chalky and firm, and a sweet wine grape at Rust.

grapes.name: Neuburger
grapes.styles: A Leithaberg DAC white, nutty and broad, and an old Rust grape for Ausbruch.

grapes.name: Grüner Veltliner
grapes.styles: The fourth Leithaberg DAC white, fuller and softer here than on the Danube.

grapes.name: St. Laurent
grapes.styles: Silky, fragrant Pinot relative, grown around the lake and allowed in Leithaberg DAC red blends.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Blauburgunder on the Leithaberg's limestone and in the Seewinkel, light and fine, a minor partner in Leithaberg DAC red.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: Planted around the lake for the Pannonian blends, where it softens Blaufränkisch and Zweigelt.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: A blending grape of the lakeside estates' international cuvées, ripening well in the Pannonian heat.

grapes.name: Furmint
grapes.styles: The Tokaj grape, an old Rust variety revived for Ruster Ausbruch and for dry whites.

wines.note: Blaufränkisch from Deutschkreutz, Horitschon, Neckenmarkt and Lutzmannsburg: dark cherry, pepper and firm tannin on clay; Klassik is fresh and unoaked, Ried and Reserve bottlings are cask aged and need five years. Pour with duck, lamb and game.

Blaufränkisch, at least 85%, from the limestone and schist of the west shore: finer, cooler and more mineral than Mittelburgenland's, with a red fruited lift. Leithaberg DAC white is Weissburgunder, Chardonnay, Neuburger or Grüner Veltliner, alone or blended, dry and chalky.
Blaufränkisch from the slate and iron soils of Südburgenland: taut, savoury, graphite and sour cherry, lighter in body than the north and long lived.
Zweigelt from the east shore: juicy cherry and soft tannin as Klassik, served cool with charcuterie; the Reserve is at least 60% Zweigelt, cask aged and fuller.

Rust's botrytis wine, picked by hand at 30° KMW, at least 45 grams of residual sugar and usually far more: apricot, honey, orange peel and saffron with bright acidity. Serve cold, in small pours, with blue cheese, foie gras or an apricot tart.

From Illmitz and Apetlon, Welschriesling and Chardonnay most often, picked shrivelled with noble rot: dense, honeyed and fresh, the equal of Sauternes and Tokaj. Beerenauslese and Auslese are its lighter rungs.
Reed wine: healthy grapes dried on reed mats from the lake shore for at least three months before pressing, the Austrian Strohwein made with the local reeds; at least 25° KMW.
Grapes frozen on the vine and pressed frozen at 25° KMW, clean and racy rather than botrytised; the Seewinkel's cold winter nights make it most years.

made.viticulture: Burgenland farms flat land around the lake and gentle hills elsewhere, so it is largely machine worked except on the Leithaberg's slopes, at Rust and on the Eisenberg. The Seewinkel's vines stand on sand and gravel a metre or so above the water table, cooled by the lake and the wind, and the sweet wine estates leave Welschriesling, Chardonnay, Weissburgunder and Muskateller to hang into November for botrytis, picking berry by berry over several passes; Ruster Ausbruch DAC demands hand picking of shrivelled, botrytised berries. Schilfwein growers pick healthy grapes and lay them on reed mats in airy lofts for three months or more. Zweigelt yields generously and must be kept in check for Reserve wines; Blaufränkisch, late ripening and vigorous, is planted on the heavier clay of Mittelburgenland and the schist of the Eisenberg, where its tannins soften only with full ripeness. Frost is rare near the lake, but hail and summer drought are not. Organic and biodynamic farming are widespread around the lake, and the Pannobile growers of Gols, formed in 1994, set a standard for the Seewinkel's reds.
made.winemaking: Red winemaking here follows the modern Austrian pattern: destemmed fruit, controlled fermentation in steel or open vats, a few weeks on skins for the Reserves, malolactic conversion and ageing in large old casks or in barriques, with the fashion for new oak that marked the 1990s now in retreat. Mittelburgenland DAC Klassik is unoaked and fresh; its Ried and Reserve wines are aged in cask and released later with at least 13% alcohol. Leithaberg DAC red must be at least 85% Blaufränkisch, with Zweigelt, St. Laurent or Pinot Noir allowed as partners, and is released in the September of the second year. The sweet wines are made as they are at Tokaj and Sauternes: botrytised berries pressed slowly, long cool fermentations that stop of themselves, then months in cask or steel; Ruster Ausbruch DAC must be made in a Rust cellar from Rust's own white grapes and carry at least 45 grams of residual sugar. Eiswein is pressed frozen. No Prädikatswein may be chaptalised or sweetened.

law.classification: Burgenland is one of Austria's four generic wine growing regions and holds six DACs as of 2026, more than any other state. Mittelburgenland DAC (2005 vintage) and Eisenberg DAC (2009 vintage) are Blaufränkisch alone; Leithaberg DAC (red from 2008, white from 2009) is Blaufränkisch led red and four grape white; Neusiedlersee DAC (created in 2012) is Zweigelt; Rosalia DAC (created in 2018) is Blaufränkisch or Zweigelt red and a rosé from any Qualitätswein red grape; Ruster Ausbruch DAC (2020 vintage) is botrytised sweet wine from Rust at Trockenbeerenauslese ripeness. The sweet wines of the Seewinkel are labelled by the national Prädikat ladder, Beerenauslese at 25° KMW, Trockenbeerenauslese at 30, Eiswein and Schilfwein at 25. Anything else is Burgenland Qualitätswein.
tiers: Mittelburgenland DAC
Blaufränkisch only: Klassik 12.5 to 13% alcohol and unoaked; with a Ried name or as Reserve at least 13%, cask aged, released later.
Leithaberg DAC
Red: at least 85% Blaufränkisch with Zweigelt, St. Laurent or Pinot Noir, at least 12.5%; white: Weissburgunder, Chardonnay, Neuburger, Grüner Veltliner alone or blended.
Eisenberg DAC
Blaufränkisch only from Südburgenland: Klassik at least 12.5%, Reserve at least 13% and cask aged.
Neusiedlersee DAC
Zweigelt: Klassik at least 12%; Reserve at least 13%, at least 60% Zweigelt in a blend with other local reds, aged before release.
Rosalia DAC
Blaufränkisch or Zweigelt reds and a dry rosé from any Qualitätswein red grape, from the Rosalia hills between the lake and Mittelburgenland; created in 2018.
Ruster Ausbruch DAC
Botrytised sweet wine from white grapes grown and made in Rust, hand picked at 30° KMW, at least 45 g/l residual sugar; from the 2020 vintage the only lawful use of the word Ausbruch.
Prädikatswein
The Seewinkel's sweet ladder: Auslese 21° KMW, Beerenauslese 25, Eiswein 25, Strohwein or Schilfwein 25, Trockenbeerenauslese 30.
labels: Literally broken out: the shrivelled berries picked out of the bunch; today lawful only as Ruster Ausbruch DAC.
Reed wine: Strohwein dried on reed mats cut from the lake shore.
The lake corner: the flat east shore around Illmitz, Apetlon and Podersdorf.
A growers' group of Gols formed in 1994 whose members bottle a Pannobile red from local grapes under one label.
Südburgenland's rustic wine from American hybrid vines, strawberry scented, tolerated locally under its own rules.

places.name: Neusiedlersee
places.note: The region of the lake's east and north shores: Zweigelt reds under Neusiedlersee DAC, Pannonian blends from Gols, and the great botrytis sweet wines of the Seewinkel.

places.name: Illmitz
places.note: In the Seewinkel between the lake and the salt pans, the capital of Austrian sweet wine: Welschriesling and Chardonnay Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese from shrivelled, botrytised berries, with the lake's mists on one side and the national park's reed beds on the other.

places.name: Apetlon and Podersdorf
places.note: Illmitz's neighbours in the Seewinkel, Apetlon for sweet wines and Schilfwein, Podersdorf on the shore with Zweigelt on sand and gravel.

places.name: Gols
places.note: The largest wine village of Burgenland on the lake's northern shore, home of the Pannobile growers and of the state's most ambitious reds, Zweigelt, Blaufränkisch and blends.

places.name: Mönchhof, Frauenkirchen and Halbturn
places.note: The villages behind the Seewinkel towards the Hungarian border, on gravel and loam, with reds and the sweet wines of estates that farm towards Illmitz.

places.name: Leithaberg
places.note: The west shore from Jois and Winden south through Purbach, Donnerskirchen and Eisenstadt to Grosshöflein, where the Leitha range's limestone and mica schist give Burgenland's most mineral whites and finest Blaufränkisch under Leithaberg DAC.

places.name: Purbach and Donnerskirchen
places.note: The slope villages of the west shore above the reeds, limestone and schist terraces for Leithaberg DAC Blaufränkisch and Weissburgunder, among the oldest vineyards of the lake.

places.name: Eisenstadt and Grosshöflein
places.note: The state capital, the Esterházy princes' seat, and the hill village beside it, where the Leithaberg turns away from the lake and the reds take on limestone grip.

places.name: Rust
places.note: The free town on the west shore, granted its freedom in 1681 against a payment that included Ausbruch wine: botrytised Ruster Ausbruch DAC from Welschriesling, Weissburgunder, Chardonnay, Furmint and Muskateller on limestone and schist, and serious Blaufränkisch from the Mariental vineyard.

places.name: Rosalia
places.note: The hills south west of the lake around Mattersburg and Pöttelsdorf, between the Leithaberg and Mittelburgenland: Rosalia DAC for Blaufränkisch and Zweigelt reds and a dry rosé, since 2018.

places.name: Mittelburgenland
places.note: The Blaufränkischland: a warm basin of heavy clay and loam open to Hungary, with Deutschkreutz, Horitschon, Neckenmarkt and Lutzmannsburg as its four villages and Mittelburgenland DAC, Blaufränkisch alone, since the 2005 vintage; the weightiest and most structured Blaufränkisch in Austria.

places.name: Deutschkreutz
places.note: The largest of the four villages, on the Hungarian border opposite Sopron, with the Goldberg site and the densest, darkest Blaufränkisch.

places.name: Horitschon
places.note: On the western edge of the basin, loam over clay, a touch fresher; the Hochäcker and Dürrau Rieden are its names.

places.name: Neckenmarkt and Lutzmannsburg
places.note: Neckenmarkt to the north under the Ödenburg hills with old vines on loam; Lutzmannsburg in the south by the Rabnitz river with its own old vine Blaufränkisch.

places.name: Eisenberg and Südburgenland
places.note: The far south along the Pinka valley by the Hungarian border: the Eisenberg and the Csaterberg above Deutsch Schützen and Eisenberg an der Pinka, green schist, slate and iron rich loam, Eisenberg DAC Blaufränkisch since the 2009 vintage, taut and savoury; Rechnitz to the north and the Uhudler country around the Pinkatal.

producers.name: Weinlaubenhof Kracher
producers.why: Illmitz; the Seewinkel's sweet wine reference, numbered Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese cuvées in two lines, Zwischen den Seen in steel and Nouvelle Vague in barrique.

producers.name: Feiler-Artinger
producers.why: Rust; Ruster Ausbruch of great purity and Blaufränkisch and Pannonian blends from the Leithaberg's limestone.

producers.name: Ernst Triebaumer
producers.why: Rust; the Mariental Blaufränkisch that in the 1980s proved the grape could make a great dry red, beside classic Ausbruch.

producers.name: Moric
producers.why: Mittelburgenland; old vine Blaufränkisch from Neckenmarkt and Lutzmannsburg made with whole bunches and old casks, the Burgundian reading of the grape.

producers.name: Gesellmann
producers.why: Deutschkreutz; Mittelburgenland's benchmark for Blaufränkisch Reserve and for the G cuvée, cask aged and long lived.

producers.name: Weninger
producers.why: Horitschon; biodynamic Blaufränkisch from Mittelburgenland's Rieden and from across the border in Sopron.

producers.name: Umathum
producers.why: Frauenkirchen; biodynamic Zweigelt, St. Laurent and Blaufränkisch from the Seewinkel's gravel, among the lake's most elegant reds.

producers.name: Velich
producers.why: Apetlon; the Tiglat Chardonnay that showed the Seewinkel could make a great dry white, beside Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese.

producers.name: Kollwentz
producers.why: Grosshöflein; the Leithaberg's limestone, Chardonnay and Blaufränkisch, and the Steinzeiler cuvée, a leader of the modern Burgenland since the 1980s.

producers.name: Prieler
producers.why: Schützen am Gebirge; Leithaberg DAC Blaufränkisch and Weissburgunder from the Goldberg's schist, fine and mineral.

producers.name: Esterházy
producers.why: Eisenstadt and Trausdorf; the princely estate, Leithaberg and lakeside wines under a name a server will recognise from Haydn's court.

producers.name: Wachter-Wiesler
producers.why: Deutsch Schützen; Eisenberg DAC Blaufränkisch from the slate and iron soils of the far south, the region's standard bearer.

exam: Place the Neusiedlersee and explain its botrytis: a shallow steppe lake, warm, misty autumn mornings, noble rot nearly every year.
Name the six Burgenland DACs with their grapes and years: Mittelburgenland 2005, Leithaberg 2008 and 2009, Eisenberg 2009, Neusiedlersee 2012, Rosalia 2018, Ruster Ausbruch 2020.
Know Ruster Ausbruch DAC: Rust only, hand picked botrytised berries, 30° KMW, at least 45 g/l residual sugar, from the 2020 vintage.
Tell Blaufränkisch from Zweigelt by structure and by home: clay of Mittelburgenland and schist of Eisenberg against the sand of the Seewinkel.
Name the Seewinkel villages, Illmitz, Apetlon and Podersdorf, and Gols as the reds village.
Know Schilfwein as reed dried Strohwein and the Prädikat weights of 25 and 30° KMW.
Hold the soils: sand and gravel by the lake, limestone and mica schist on the Leithaberg, clay in Mittelburgenland, slate and iron at the Eisenberg.
traps: Ausbruch is no longer a Prädikat between Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese; since the 2020 vintage it exists only as Ruster Ausbruch DAC at 30° KMW, Trockenbeerenauslese ripeness.
Neusiedlersee DAC is Zweigelt, not the sweet wines; the Seewinkel's Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese are Prädikatswein, not DAC.
Leithaberg DAC red must be at least 85% Blaufränkisch, so a Leithaberg Zweigelt is Burgenland Qualitätswein.
Mittelburgenland and Eisenberg DAC are Blaufränkisch alone; Rosalia DAC admits Zweigelt and rosé as well.
Rust lies on the west shore with the Leithaberg, not in the Seewinkel; Illmitz is across the water on the east.
Schilfwein is dried on reed mats and is a Strohwein; it is not botrytised and it is not Eiswein.
Zweigelt is the most planted grape of Burgenland and of the Seewinkel; Blaufränkisch leads Mittelburgenland and the south.

cards.f: Burgenland's six DACs: grape and year
cards.b: Mittelburgenland 2005 (Blaufränkisch), Leithaberg 2008 red and 2009 white (Blaufränkisch; four whites), Eisenberg 2009 (Blaufränkisch), Neusiedlersee 2012 (Zweigelt), Rosalia 2018 (reds and rosé), Ruster Ausbruch 2020 (sweet).
A steppe lake about 36 km long and one to two metres deep: it warms fast, holds warmth into autumn, and its morning mists burn off by midday, the humid then dry cycle noble rot needs.
From the 2020 vintage: white grapes grown and vinified in Rust, hand picked botrytised berries at 30° KMW, at least 45 g/l residual sugar. The only lawful Ausbruch.

cards.f: Blaufränkisch versus Zweigelt on the palate
cards.b: Blaufränkisch: dark cherry, black pepper, iron, high acid, firm tannin, ages. Zweigelt: sour cherry, soft tannin, juicy, drink young; its parent is Blaufränkisch.

cards.f: Leithaberg DAC red: the blend rule
cards.b: At least 85% Blaufränkisch, with Zweigelt, St. Laurent or Pinot Noir as partners; at least 12.5% alcohol; released in the September of the second year.
Seewinkel: sand, gravel, loam, salt pans. Leithaberg: Leitha limestone and mica schist. Mittelburgenland: heavy clay and loam. Eisenberg: green schist, slate, iron rich loam.
Reed wine: healthy grapes dried at least three months on reed mats from the lake, pressed at 25° KMW or more; Austria's Strohwein in the Seewinkel's version. Not botrytised.

cards.f: The Seewinkel's villages and the reds village
cards.b: Illmitz, Apetlon and Podersdorf on the east shore for sweet wines; Gols on the north shore for Zweigelt, Blaufränkisch and the Pannobile blends.
A free town since 1681 on the west shore, limestone and schist, home of Ruster Ausbruch DAC and of the Mariental Blaufränkisch.

questions.q: Which grape is named by the Mittelburgenland DAC?
questions.exp: Mittelburgenland is the Blaufränkischland and its DAC, from the 2005 vintage, admits Blaufränkisch alone; Zweigelt is the Neusiedlersee DAC's grape.

questions.q: What is the minimum must weight, in KMW, for Ruster Ausbruch DAC?
questions.exp: Since the 2020 vintage Ruster Ausbruch DAC is picked at 30° KMW, the same as Trockenbeerenauslese, from hand picked botrytised berries grown and made in Rust.

questions.q: Which grape does the Neusiedlersee DAC protect?
questions.exp: Neusiedlersee DAC, created in 2012, is a red from Zweigelt, Klassik and Reserve; the lake's sweet wines from Welschriesling and Chardonnay are Prädikatswein outside the DAC.

questions.q: On which shore of the Neusiedlersee does the Seewinkel lie?
questions.exp: The Seewinkel, the lake corner, is the flat east shore around Illmitz, Apetlon and Podersdorf; Rust and the Leithaberg are on the west shore.

questions.q: What is the minimum share of Blaufränkisch in a Leithaberg DAC red?
questions.exp: Leithaberg DAC red is at least 85% Blaufränkisch with Zweigelt, St. Laurent or Pinot Noir as partners; 60% is the Zweigelt floor of a Neusiedlersee DAC Reserve blend.

questions.q: What is a Schilfwein dried on before pressing?
questions.exp: Schilfwein is the Seewinkel's Strohwein, healthy grapes dried on mats of reed cut from the lake shore for at least three months before pressing at 25° KMW or above.

questions.q: Which village is the capital of the Seewinkel's sweet wines?
questions.exp: Illmitz, between the lake and the salt pans, is where the Seewinkel's Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese are made; Gols is the reds village, Rust the Ausbruch town across the water and Deutschkreutz the heart of Mittelburgenland.

questions.q: Which Burgenland DAC names Blaufränkisch from the slate soils of the far south?
questions.exp: Eisenberg DAC, from the 2009 vintage, covers Südburgenland's Blaufränkisch on green schist, slate and iron rich loam along the Pinka; Leithaberg is limestone and schist by the lake, Rosalia the hills between.

regions.name: Steiermark (Styria)
regions.summary: Steiermark, Styria, is Austria's green south east: steep, wooded hills south of Graz running to the Slovenian border, wetter than the Danube and worked almost entirely by hand. It is white wine country of a different kind, Sauvignon Blanc above all, with Chardonnay under its local name Morillon, Gelber Muskateller, Welschriesling and Weissburgunder, all dry. Three regions share it: Südsteiermark along the border, the land of Gamlitz and the great Rieden; Vulkanland Steiermark to the east on old volcanoes, with Traminer at Klöch; Weststeiermark around Stainz and Deutschlandsberg, home of Schilcher, the piercing rosé of Blauer Wildbacher. Each has had a DAC since the 2018 vintage, built on the origin pyramid of Gebietswein, Ortswein and Riedenwein.

terroir.climate: Illyrian, the Austrians say: a Mediterranean influence over the Alps' southern edge, with warm, humid summers, far more rain than the Danube or Burgenland, mild autumns and cold winters. Thunderstorms and hail are the growing hazards, and the humidity keeps growers on steep, airy slopes. Nights are cool and the harvest runs from mid September into October, late for Austria, which gives the Sauvignon Blanc its aromatic lift and its acidity.
terroir.soils: Südsteiermark lies on opok, a calcareous marl that crumbles like slate when dry, with sand, gravel and limestone conglomerate on the lower hills and schist and gneiss in the Sausal around Kitzeck. Vulkanland Steiermark sits on the basalt, tuff and volcanic ash of the extinct volcanoes at Klöch, Kapfenstein and Straden, over sand and loam. Weststeiermark is gneiss and schist of the Koralpe's crystalline rock, acid and poor, which the Blauer Wildbacher likes.
terroir.topography: The steepest vineyards in Austria outside the Wachau: hills with slopes of 30 to 50 per cent and steeper south of Graz, ridges running north to south towards Slovenia with vines on the warm flanks and forest on the cold ones, and the Sausal rising to Kitzeck at about 560 metres, among the highest wine villages in Europe. The Vulkanland is gentler, cones and ridges of old volcanoes above the Raab valley; the Weststeiermark is the eastern foot of the Koralpe above the Mur plain.
terroir.water: The Mur runs through Graz and south along the border, marking the Südsteiermark's eastern edge and bringing cool air up its valley; the Raab and the Sulm are the other rivers. The damp Illyrian air itself matters more than any one river, breeding mildew and the need for open, well drained slopes.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Styria's signature and leading grape: gooseberry, elderflower, nettle and wet stone in the fresh Klassik style, dense, smoky and long lived from the classified Rieden of the Südsteiermark, always dry.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Called Morillon here and treated as a local grape: lean, mineral and unoaked at the base, richer and cask aged from the Rieden, with a green apple and hazelnut character on opok and limestone.

grapes.name: Welschriesling
grapes.styles: Widely planted, light, crisp and neutral, the everyday Buschenschank white and the base of Styrian spritzers.

grapes.name: Gelber Muskateller
grapes.styles: Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains made dry: fragrant with orange blossom and elderflower, light and sharp, Styria's aperitif grape.

grapes.name: Pinot Blanc
grapes.styles: Weissburgunder: creamy, quiet, a classic Styrian white and a strand of the Ortswein ranges.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris / Grigio
grapes.styles: Grauburgunder, full and spicy, grown on the Vulkanland's loam and in the Südsteiermark.

grapes.name: Traminer
grapes.styles: The Klöch speciality of the Vulkanland, Gewürztraminer, Roter and Gelber Traminer on volcanic soil: rose petal, lychee and spice, dry to off dry.

grapes.name: Blauer Wildbacher
grapes.styles: The Weststeiermark's red grape, nearly all of it made as Schilcher, a pale, high acid rosé of redcurrant and rhubarb, still or sparkling, with a small amount made as light red.

grapes.name: Zweigelt
grapes.styles: A little red for the Buschenschank table across all three regions.

wines.note: Dry, taut, gooseberry and elderflower over crushed stone: the Gebietswein is the fresh pour, the Ortswein from Gamlitz or Ehrenhausen fuller, and the Riedenwein from Zieregg or Kranachberg a dense, smoky wine for ageing. Pour with asparagus, goat's cheese, trout and the Styrian pumpkin seed oil salad.
Styrian Chardonnay, lean and mineral as Klassik, nutty and cask aged from the Rieden; a server should know the word is Chardonnay and nothing else.
Dry Muscat with orange blossom and grapefruit, light and sharp; Styria's summer aperitif and the match for a spring vegetable plate.
The Weststeiermark's rosé from Blauer Wildbacher: pale pink, redcurrant and rhubarb, searing acidity, drunk young and cold with Styrian fried chicken; also made sparkling and as Sturm in autumn.
The Klöch speciality on basalt: rose and lychee scented, spicy, often with a little residual sugar, a match for Asian spice and washed rind cheese.
The young wine of the year, released each November under a shared label, light and fruity, Styria's answer to the Heuriger wine.

made.viticulture: Styria is hand work on steep ground. Slopes of 30 per cent and more on opok and schist are terraced only where they must be, and most vines stand in rows running straight up the hill, picked by hand and carried out in crates. The Klapotetz, a wooden wind rattle on a tall post, still turns in the vineyards each autumn to scare the birds, and has become the region's emblem. Humidity is the enemy: mildew pressure is high, hail comes most summers somewhere in the hills, and growers choose airy ridge tops and keep canopies open. Sauvignon Blanc is picked in several passes from mid September, early for the fresh style and later for the Rieden; Blauer Wildbacher in the west is picked early to hold its acidity for Schilcher. Yields for the DAC Riedenwein are hand harvested by rule and lower than for the Gebietswein. Organic and biodynamic estates are common, and a few growers in the Südsteiermark have become known for long skin maceration and natural wine, outside the DAC. The vineyards sit in a patchwork of forest, orchard and pumpkin field, and the Buschenschank at the top of the hill sells the wine with cold cuts and the seed oil.
made.winemaking: Two styles run side by side. The Klassik, the style the growers' association Steirische Terroir und Klassik Weingüter carries in its name, is picked fresh, pressed gently, fermented cool in stainless steel, kept on fine lees briefly and bottled early, dry and aromatic, with no oak and no malolactic conversion. The Rieden wines are picked riper, often whole bunch pressed, fermented and aged in large old oak or acacia casks, left on lees for a year or more and released late; the DAC sets a release of May of the second year for Riedenwein and allows wood as long as it does not dominate. Morillon follows the same two paths. Schilcher is pressed quickly off the skins for a pale colour and fermented cool, dry, with searing acidity, and a growing share is made into Sekt. Traminer at Klöch may keep a few grams of sugar. Every Styrian DAC wine is made from the listed grapes, alone or as a cuvée, and is dry as a rule, with Traminer the allowed exception: Sauvignon Blanc, Morillon, Weissburgunder, Grauburgunder, Riesling, Gelber Muskateller, Welschriesling and Traminer on the list and Blauer Wildbacher added for Schilcher in the west.

law.classification: Steiermark is one of Austria's four generic wine growing regions and holds three regional DACs, all created for the 2018 vintage on the origin pyramid rather than the older Klassik and Reserve: Südsteiermark DAC, Vulkanland Steiermark DAC and Weststeiermark DAC. Each has a Gebietswein from the region's listed grapes, an Ortswein from named villages (Gamlitz, Leutschach, Kitzeck-Sausal, Ehrenhausen and Eichberg in the south; Klöch, Kapfenstein, Straden, St. Anna, Tieschen and others in the Vulkanland; Stainz, Deutschlandsberg, Ligist and Eibiswald in the west) and a hand picked Riedenwein from registered single vineyards released from May of the second year. Schilcher from Blauer Wildbacher is the Weststeiermark's speciality, and the name Schilcherland DAC also appears on Schilcher from the region. The Vulkanland was called Südoststeiermark until 2016. Wines outside the rules are Steiermark Qualitätswein.
tiers: Gebietswein
Regional wine of Südsteiermark, Vulkanland Steiermark or Weststeiermark DAC from the listed grapes, dry, fresh; released from the March after harvest.
Ortswein
Village wine from a named Styrian wine village such as Gamlitz, Kitzeck-Sausal, Klöch or Stainz, from the listed grapes, released later and fuller.
Riedenwein
Single vineyard wine, Ried before the name, hand picked, released from May of the second year; Zieregg, Kranachberg, Grassnitzberg and Obegg are the famous ones.
Schilcherland DAC
A DAC name carried by Schilcher, the Blauer Wildbacher rosé of the Weststeiermark, beside Weststeiermark DAC.
Steiermark Qualitätswein
Everything outside the DACs: other grapes, sweeter styles, long macerated wines and most Sturm and Junker.
labels: The rosé of Blauer Wildbacher from the Weststeiermark, named for its shimmering colour.
The growers' word for the fresh, unoaked, early bottled style, from the STK association.
STK, Erste and Grosse STK Ried
The Steirische Terroir und Klassik Weingüter's private classification of its members' top vineyards in two ranks.
The young wine of the vintage released under a shared Styrian label each November.
The wooden wind rattle of the Styrian vineyards, the region's emblem.

places.name: Südsteiermark
places.note: The southern hills along the Slovenian border from Leutschach to Ehrenhausen and north to the Sausal: opok marl, sand and limestone, Sauvignon Blanc, Morillon and Muskateller, Südsteiermark DAC since 2018 and the steepest, most classified vineyards of the state.

places.name: Gamlitz
places.note: The largest wine village of the Südsteiermark, between Leutschach and the Mur, with the Kranachberg, Sernauberg and Eckberg Rieden and many of the region's leading estates.

places.name: Ehrenhausen and Berghausen
places.note: On the Mur at the border, where the Zieregg rises on opok and limestone above the river, the Südsteiermark's most famous single vineyard for Sauvignon Blanc and Morillon; Ratsch and Spielfeld lie beside it with the Grassnitzberg and Hochgrassnitzberg.

places.name: Leutschach
places.note: The western end of the border hills, higher and cooler, with the Pössnitzberg Ried and a reputation for taut Sauvignon Blanc and Morillon.

places.name: Kitzeck im Sausal
places.note: The Sausal hills north of the border on schist and gneiss, with Kitzeck at about 560 metres among the highest wine villages in Europe: Riesling and Sauvignon Blanc with a slate edge, and the Ortswein name Kitzeck-Sausal.

places.name: Vulkanland Steiermark
places.note: The south east, Südoststeiermark until 2016: the cones and ridges of extinct volcanoes at Klöch, Kapfenstein, Straden, Tieschen, St. Anna am Aigen and Riegersburg, basalt and tuff over loam, Vulkanland Steiermark DAC since 2018, with Traminer at Klöch and Sauvignon Blanc, Morillon, Grauburgunder and Weissburgunder elsewhere.

places.name: Klöch
places.note: The volcanic hill on the Slovenian border known for Traminer in all its colours, dry to sweet, on basalt; the Vulkanland's one village tied to a single grape in the public mind.

places.name: Kapfenstein and Straden
places.note: Kapfenstein's castle on its volcanic cone and Straden to the west, the heart of the Vulkanland for Sauvignon Blanc, Morillon and Grauburgunder from basalt and tuff.

places.name: Weststeiermark
places.note: The eastern foot of the Koralpe west of the Mur, from Ligist through Stainz and Deutschlandsberg to Eibiswald: gneiss and schist, Blauer Wildbacher and its Schilcher rosé above all, Weststeiermark DAC since 2018 with the Schilcherland DAC name beside it, and a small share of whites.

places.name: Stainz
places.note: The market town at the region's heart, Schilcherland's capital, with the Schilcher Buschenschank trail through its hills.

places.name: Deutschlandsberg
places.note: Under the Koralpe's slopes further south, the Weststeiermark's largest wine town, Blauer Wildbacher on schist for Schilcher still and sparkling.

producers.name: Tement
producers.why: Berghausen; the Zieregg Sauvignon Blanc and Morillon that put the Südsteiermark on the world's lists, with holdings across the border in Slovenia.

producers.name: Polz
producers.why: Spielfeld; a large family estate of the border hills, Hochgrassnitzberg Sauvignon Blanc and a reliable Klassik range.

producers.name: Sattlerhof
producers.why: Gamlitz; Kranachberg and Sernauberg Sauvignon Blanc and Morillon, among the region's finest.

producers.name: Gross
producers.why: Ratsch; Nussberg and Sulz Sauvignon Blanc of precision, the quiet classicist of the Südsteiermark.

producers.name: Lackner-Tinnacher
producers.why: Gamlitz; Sauvignon Blanc, Morillon and Muskateller from the Steinbach and Welles Rieden, finely drawn.

producers.name: Wohlmuth
producers.why: Kitzeck im Sausal; the Sausal's leading estate, Riesling and Sauvignon Blanc from the slate of the Edelschuh and Steinriegl, among Austria's steepest sites.

producers.name: Neumeister
producers.why: Straden; the Vulkanland's reference for Sauvignon Blanc, Morillon and Grauburgunder on volcanic soil, with the Saziani Riedenwein.

producers.name: Winkler-Hermaden
producers.why: Kapfenstein; the castle estate on the volcanic cone, Sauvignon Blanc and the Olivin Zweigelt from basalt.

producers.name: Langmann
producers.why: St. Stefan ob Stainz; the Weststeiermark's Schilcher benchmark, still and sparkling, with a serious Riedenwein from Blauer Wildbacher.

exam: Place Steiermark in the south east, south of Graz against Slovenia, and know it as Austria's wettest, steepest and most Mediterranean region.
Name the three regions and their DACs, all from the 2018 vintage: Südsteiermark, Vulkanland Steiermark, Weststeiermark, built as Gebietswein, Ortswein, Riedenwein.
Know Morillon is Chardonnay and Schilcher is a rosé of Blauer Wildbacher from the Weststeiermark.
Hold Sauvignon Blanc as the signature grape and the Südsteiermark as its home, with Gamlitz and the Zieregg as its names.
Give the soils: opok marl in the south, basalt and tuff in the Vulkanland, gneiss and schist in the west and the Sausal.
Know Klöch for Traminer and the Vulkanland's old name, Südoststeiermark, changed in 2016.
Describe the Illyrian climate and why humidity, hail and steep slopes shape the farming.
traps: Morillon is Chardonnay and nothing else; it is not a local grape and not related to Mondeuse or Morio-Muskat.
Schilcher is a rosé of Blauer Wildbacher, not a white and not a Pinot; it comes from the Weststeiermark alone.
The Styrian DACs name no single grape: they are origin pyramids with a list of grapes, unlike Weinviertel DAC or Mittelburgenland DAC.
Steirische Klassik is a growers' style word, not a legal tier; Klassik is a legal rung only in the older DACs of the Danube and Burgenland.
Kitzeck im Sausal is in the Südsteiermark, not the Weststeiermark, on schist rather than opok.
Vulkanland Steiermark and Südoststeiermark are the same region under its new and old names, not two regions.
Styrian Sauvignon Blanc is dry and often lees aged or cask aged at the Ried level; do not expect Marlborough's sweetness of fruit.

cards.f: Styria's three regions and what each is known for
cards.b: Südsteiermark: Sauvignon Blanc, Morillon, Muskateller on opok (Gamlitz, Zieregg). Vulkanland Steiermark: basalt, Traminer at Klöch. Weststeiermark: Schilcher rosé from Blauer Wildbacher on gneiss and schist.

cards.f: The Styrian DACs: year and shape
cards.b: All three from the 2018 vintage, on the origin pyramid: Gebietswein, Ortswein (named villages), Riedenwein (hand picked, released from May of the second year). No single grape; a list of nine.
Chardonnay under its Styrian name, treated as a local grape: lean, mineral and unoaked at the base, nutty and cask aged from the Rieden. Nothing else.
A pale, high acid rosé of Blauer Wildbacher from the Weststeiermark alone: redcurrant and rhubarb, drunk young and cold, still or sparkling.
Klassik: fresh, steel, gooseberry, elderflower, nettle, early bottled. Riedenwein: riper, whole bunch pressed, large old casks, long lees, smoky and dense, built to age.
Südsteiermark: opok (calcareous marl), sand, gravel, conglomerate; schist and gneiss in the Sausal. Vulkanland: basalt, tuff, volcanic ash. Weststeiermark: gneiss and schist of the Koralpe.
Mediterranean warmth over the Alps' southern edge: humid summers, high rainfall, hail, mild autumns, cold winters; steep airy slopes and hand work follow from it.

cards.f: Vulkanland Steiermark's old name and date
cards.b: Südoststeiermark, renamed Vulkanland Steiermark in 2016 for its extinct volcanoes at Klöch, Kapfenstein, Straden and Riegersburg.
The wooden wind rattle on a tall post that turns in Styrian vineyards each autumn to scare birds off the ripening grapes; the region's emblem.
The young wine of the vintage, released each November under a shared Styrian label: light, fruity, Styria's answer to the Heuriger wine.

questions.q: Which grape is sold under the name Morillon in Steiermark?
questions.exp: Morillon is the Styrian name for Chardonnay, made lean and mineral or cask aged from the Rieden; the other three are grown in Styria under their own names.

questions.q: From which grape is Schilcher made?
questions.exp: Schilcher is the pale, high acid rosé of Blauer Wildbacher, the red grape of the Weststeiermark around Stainz and Deutschlandsberg; a little is also made red and sparkling.

questions.q: From which vintage have the three Styrian DACs applied?
questions.exp: Südsteiermark, Vulkanland Steiermark and Weststeiermark DAC were all created for the 2018 vintage; 2016 was the year Südoststeiermark was renamed Vulkanland and 2020 the Wachau's DAC vintage.

questions.q: What is opok, the soil of the Südsteiermark's hills?
questions.exp: Opok is the local name for a calcareous marl that dries hard and splits like slate; it holds water in the Südsteiermark's wet climate and gives the Sauvignon Blanc its stony edge.

questions.q: Which Vulkanland Steiermark village is famous for Traminer?
questions.exp: Klöch's basalt slopes on the Slovenian border are the home of Styrian Traminer; Gamlitz and Kitzeck are Südsteiermark villages and Stainz is the Schilcher town of the west.

questions.q: Which soil marks the vineyards of Vulkanland Steiermark?
questions.exp: Vulkanland Steiermark, called Südoststeiermark until 2016, sits on the basalt, tuff and ash of extinct volcanoes at Klöch, Kapfenstein and Straden. Opok marl is the Südsteiermark's soil, gneiss and schist belong to the Weststeiermark and the Sausal, and loess to the Danube and the Weinviertel.

questions.q: Which grape is the signature of the Südsteiermark?
questions.exp: Sauvignon Blanc is Styria's flag, grown on the opok hills of Gamlitz, Ehrenhausen and Leutschach; Grüner Veltliner belongs to the Danube and Traminer to Klöch in the Vulkanland.

questions.q: Which Muscat variety does Steiermark make as a dry, fragrant aperitif white?
questions.exp: Gelber Muskateller is Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains under its Austrian name, made bone dry in Styria with orange blossom, elderflower and sharp acidity. Welschriesling is the neutral everyday white, and Traminer the Klöch speciality of the Vulkanland.
